rationale: The source's Sage is Lantana camara, a taxon distinct from culinary Salvia officinalis. Its listed uses are cooling and diabetes rather than a pain severity comparison.
The gastrointestinal review supplies no sage ingredient exposure for pain. Its other botanical formulations and epigastric symptom results have distinct compositions.
The Petroselinum crispum survey row documents infusion and decoction for other uses, including headache. It gives no specific constipation use or measured stool outcome for parsley.
Soybean oil is an allergy eligibility mention. Extrapyramidal effects are reported for pharmacologic comparisons, without refined soybean oil assigned for dyskinesia.
Hypomimia appears in the discussion of drooling and motor function. The review does not link reduced facial expressiveness with a sage exposure.
The grated nutmeg infusion is reported for upset stomach. The separate topical entry concerns headache. Neither row estimates constipation after ground nutmeg.
The parsley row includes a customary headache infusion without stating whether the material was dried. The table does not measure headache or Parkinson pain severity.
The ginger arm identified in the Phillips postoperative nausea comparison was outside the arm extraction for the network. No measured ginger-attributable dyskinesia result is present.
Processed ginger appears in the constipation formula. The dyskinesia material concerns other treatments including the DA-9701 safety report and gives no ground ginger motor estimate.
The cayenne row names sinus and diverticulitis uses and leaves preparation unfilled. It supplies no ground-cayenne pain severity measurement.
The local Bay Leaf entry is Pimenta racemosa, with cooling and other indications. The experiment's culinary Laurus nobilis and its constipation symptom do not match the survey entry.
The source mentions soybean oil in allergy screening. There is no dietary refined soybean oil exposure or attributed dystonia result.
The adjusted model compares dietary inflammatory scores with stool frequency. It gives neither a dried date variable nor an evaluated pain outcome.
The relevant Cochrane member tests a ginger–salt topical method plus acupuncture for urinary incontinence after stroke. Other adverse-event reports cannot supply a dried date pain intervention.
The assigned Daikenchuto formula comprises processed ginger, ginseng, Japanese pepper and maltose. Abdominal pain was measured for this product, without a dried date arm.
The Rikkunshi-to description contains jujube, a Ziziphus species. No dried Phoenix date exposure or pain contrast appears.
Cumin appears as a food comparator in antioxidant research. This secondary route gives no isolated ground-cumin test of stool or constipation symptoms.
The Black Cumin entry is Nigella sativa oil extract for hypertension. Cuminum cyminum and its constipation outcome are absent from the entry.
The STW5 footnote prints cumin. The documented comparison formula includes Carum carvi, so its separate gastrointestinal endpoint cannot be transferred to Cuminum cyminum.

The NHANES exposure is a pooled inflammatory score from a 24-hour recall. Table 2 estimates constipation defined by low stool frequency per score unit. There is no individual ginger term or separately evaluated grated exposure.
The general rhizome review lists constipation among historical digestive indications. It supplies no symptom measurement, comparison or Parkinson population for this use.

A 34-person trial after stroke compared usual care with or without processed ginger, ginseng and Japanese pepper in Daikenchuto. The symptom instrument and stool items improved in the open add-on group. The formula and diagnosis limit attribution and transfer.

Ten people with bloating and chronic constipation took the same processed-ginger formula. The constipation subscale fell and stool frequency and form showed no clear change. The registry confirms a single uncontrolled arm and the article excludes Parkinson disease.

The chart review reports more weekly stools after the whole multiherb formula in 33 patients with differing follow-up. Dose groups were observed retrospectively, without an untreated comparison or a grated-ginger arm.
The Liu member uses ginger–salt moxibustion plus acupuncture for daytime voiding after stroke. Route, co-intervention, population and outcome all differ from oral grated ginger and constipation.

The full network review identifies ginger arms in the postoperative nausea and vomiting search. Its constipation adverse-event summary applies to analyzed antiemetic drugs and supplies no ginger constipation estimate.

Interviewees reported grated or whole rhizome for general health and other rhizome preparations for distinct uses. Constipation is assigned to other plants. The ginger row gives no comparative bowel outcome.
The review covers ginger rhizome in other botanical applications. The customary constipation use belongs to Phyllanthus niruri and provides no bowel result for a ginger exposure.

The placebo trial outside Parkinson disease favored a global constipation measure and stool form. Changes in stool frequency, straining and incomplete evacuation were inconclusive. The mixture and registry dose discrepancy prevent direct attribution to grated ginger.

The narrative repeats the six-person Parkinson subgroup from the 2004 Daikenchuto publication. The formula contains processed ginger with other herbs. The review adds no independent cohort or grated-ginger contrast.
The Cochrane member concerns a topical ginger–salt procedure and voiding frequency. The source gives no graded rigidity finding for ginger in Parkinson disease.
The Ocimum basilicum row records an infusion used for cooling and lacks a fresh-leaf constipation result.
The basil material refers to aerial-part preparations in another research area. The described constipation use belongs to a different plant, Phyllanthus niruri.
The study compares a dietary inflammatory score with low stool frequency. Mentions of abdominal discomfort are background, with no grated ginger or pain analysis.

The review cites Black's separate capsule trials using unheated and heated ground ginger for provoked elbow exercise pain. The original pairing is off-population, with capsule exposure and exercise injury as the endpoint context.

The poststroke formula trial's constipation instrument contains painful evacuation and abdominal pain items. The total score and listed specific improvements supply no graded change for pain from grated ginger.

The face-scale abdominal pain result had p=.039 and the GSRS pain subscale was inconclusive. Both describe a before–after series receiving a multiherb formula. Part, processing, patient group and attribution differ from the claim.
The processed-ginger-containing formula appears in a stool count chart review. Abdominal pain is a safety item with zero events, without a graded pain efficacy contrast.
Ginger occurs among nausea and vomiting study leads. The postoperative analgesia and pain material belongs to other treatments and cannot be attached to those ginger arms.

Table 3 lists rhizome decoction, infusion and stew for joint or back pain. The grating detail belongs to general health. The survey records intended use without measured pain severity or a Parkinson cohort.
The narrative mentions traditional anti-arthritis use of ginger without a controlled grated-rhizome pain comparison.

Abdominal pain changed by −0.59 versus −0.13 (p=.063) for the whole formula versus placebo. The cohort had chronic constipation, and no separate ginger allocation or Parkinson pain estimate was reported.
The review documents gastric and bowel symptom trials and ginger in a multicomponent Kampo formula. Its results do not establish an independent grated-ginger pain contrast.
The inflammatory diet association uses a combined score and does not isolate ground turmeric. Pain severity is outside its measured outcomes.
The turmeric row names joint or back pain use as decoction, infusion or stew. Grinding, Parkinson status and a measured symptom change are unspecified.
The soybean oil occurrence is an allergy exclusion. The review has no refined soybean oil comparison for bradykinesia.
Grape occurrences are bibliographic or organization names. There is no assigned grape dietary exposure or anxiety outcome paired with it.
The postoperative article's constipation endpoint belongs to medication adverse-event comparisons. There is no measured raw-orange dietary contrast.
The sweet-orange entry describes blended, infusion or capsule use for immune purposes. The source supplies no raw-fruit constipation comparison.
The sweet-orange entry concerns derived oil and other botanical use. There is no raw-orange exposure evaluated for constipation.

The cited Rikkunshi-to Parkinson study concerns a compound including citrus peel and measured gastric emptying. The peel species, raw fruit preparation and constipation response cannot be inferred from the comparison.
The covered Parkinson gastrointestinal treatments include no sage fatigue comparison. Separate symptom and ingredient mentions cannot form an estimate.
The report describes ginger-related postoperative nausea studies and gives no anxiety severity outcome attributable to those ginger exposures.
Rosemary is reported as a mixed decoction with moringa for cooling. There is no isolated constipation comparison.
The clove row gives a customary decoction for toothache. It has no ground preparation, measured pain severity change or Parkinson sample.
The cumin label in the STW5 description denotes caraway according to the documented formulation. The source contains no toasted Cuminum cyminum and Parkinson dyskinesia comparison.
